description.narrative: The Sida funded programme will support the Council of Europe's (CoEs) country Action Plans in the Easter Partnership (EaP) region, i.e. Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Georgia, Moldova and Ukraine with a total suggested budget of 75 MSEK during the period 2019-2023. These Action Plans are strategic instruments which aim, through co-operation, to accompany countries in their efforts to bring legislation, institutions and practice further into line with European standards in the areas of human rights, the rule of law and democracy thus supporting countries in meeting their obligations. The intermediate outcomes expected are: 1. Eastern Partnership countries legislation, institutions and practices were further brought in line with European standards in the areas of human rights, rule of law and democracy. 2. Armenia, Azerbaijan, Georgia, Republic of Moldova and Ukraine made further progress in meeting their obligations as Council of Europe member states. Immediate outcomes: 1.1 Human rights: Human rights protection and equality are enhanced through the well-structured and coordinated implementation of human rights standards, including those on gender equality, and an improved effectiveness of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) system. 2.1 Rule of law: Democratic security is strengthened by an enhanced implementation of the existing legislation and European standards, the development of an enabling legal and institutional framework for a democratic and an improved quality of justice and efficiency in combating corruption. 3.1 Democracy: The democratisation of society is fostered through electoral integrity, strengthened local democracy and increased participation of young people in the democratic process. The focus of the Action Plans is to support: the revision of legislative and institutional frameworks in line with the CoE standards; the efficient functioning of reformed and newly established democratic institutions contributing to the implementation of the European Convention on Human Rights (ECHR) and of other Council of Europe standards.

sector.narrative: Public sector policy and administrative management

description.narrative: BELARUS 2022-2023 Sida funded a project - the so called Contact Group - with an experimental character, where the main responsibility over it laid within the CoE Director Generals office. It is a sensitive project considering the full scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation, and the fact that Belarus is an ally to the invading nation. By setting up the Contact Group within the CoE's GD Secretariat, it was possible to identify specific needs to be addressed in order to support Belarusian civil society. Some topics discussed were; trainings and educational programmes on human rights, civic education, inclusiveness, youth, gender equality and freedom of expression. Reported results: Some of the most important impacts of the activities implemented, as described in the reports general overview are: • Strengthened political dialogue • Increased knowledge on the CoE's human rights' standards • Raised awareness on the European standards on equality and non-discrimination • Updated proposal for legislation concerning equality • Increased knowledge and understanding of international and CoE's standards on gender equality and countering violence against women • Promotion of discussion amongst Belarusian journalists in exile on challenges and possible solutions • Increased capacities to advocate for youth participation and deliver human rights education. Sida and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs have actively participated in events during the implementation period, which resulted in positive conclusions. ARMENIA 2019-2023 The CoE's Action plan for Armenia is funded by several donors. Sweden contributed with €1.7 million. The Action plan contributed to the SDG Agenda 2030 by supporting goals 3, 4, 5, 10, 11, and 16. Some reported outcomes: HUMAN RIGHTS • The Public Council on the Protection and Promotion of the Rights of Persons belonging to National Minorities was officially inaugurated. • Targeted training for the Human Rights Defender's Office to effectively handle cases of hate speech and discrimination in line with European standards was carried out. • Other major achievements were the adoption of the first ethical rules for healthcare professionals along with the establishment of the Ethics Committee in the field of healthcare. • Advancements were also made in preparing the ground for the ratification of the Istanbul Convention through awareness-raising and capacity development. • Good progress was achieved in better integrating EU standards in the Armenian Criminal Code and Criminal Procedure code, which materialized in the abolition of death penalty in all circumstances. RULE OF LAW Good progress was accomplished in the adoption of an amended Judicial Code, based on joint opinions from the CoE's Directorate of Human Rights, among others. Another important achievement was the introduction of an effective evaluation system for judges. The ongoing criminal justice reform that aims at moving from a punitive to a rehabilitative approach also showed good progress as levels of imprisonment were reduced. DEMOCRACY Some progress was achieved through support to the Communities Association of Armenia (CAA) and to preparing a revised comprehensive law on local self-governance. Challenges Following the large influx of refugees coming from the Karabah region in September 2023, a refugee response package was launched along with other additional projects that addressed new needs in this context. It was not possible to implement activities in the areas of ensuring social rights and strengthening the rule of law due to lack of funding. Challenges still remained 2024 within thematic areas such as countering domestic violence, discrimination based on sexual orientation, and enhancing the protection of persons with disabilities. AZERBAIJAN 2018-2021 and 2022-2025. The CoE's ongoing Action plan for Azerbaijan 2018-2021 was funded by several donors. Swedens contribution covered the years 2019-2023 via a limited project support with a focus on CoEs cooperation with civil society. For the period 2022-2025, Sweden did not contribute. The Action plan contributed to the SDG Agenda 2030 by supporting goals 4, 5, 8, and 10. Some reported outcomes: HUMAN RIGHTS • The ratification of the Protocol no. 16 to the European Convention on Human Rights allows the Supreme Court and the Constitutional court of Azerbaijan to request expertise on ECtHR in Strasbourg. • The adoption of the National Execution Strategy and the Action plan for Execution of Judgements and Decisions of the ECtHR at project level. • The ratification of the Lanzarote Convention (the CoEs Convention on the Protection of Children against Sexual Exploitation and Sexual Abuse)was also an important achievement. RULE OF LAW One slightly positive area was the fight against corruption and money laundering, aiming at implementation of international standards. The focus was on the improvement of the legislative framework, the institutional capacities for fighting economic crime, money laundering and financing of terrorism. DEMOCRACY Training was offered to increase the capacities of journalists and social media representatives in conflict-sensitive journalism and in mitigating hate speech in the media. Judge candidates and prosecutors were trained on freedom of expression and freedom of information using relevant European Court law. It is assessed as important to know the international standards despite internal challenges. Youth organisations capacities and knowledge was supported, on topics such as promotion of human rights education and democratic youth participation.' Challenges In politically sensitive areas there was no progress to report as the authorities showed lack of readiness to engage in cooperation with the CoE on these topics. The Istanbul Convention is subject to many misconceptions in Azerbaijan, making it challenging to implement actions targeting violence against women as well as domestic violence. These misconceptions are also a threat to regional projects, diminishing the willingness of beneficiaries to participate. Awareness raising initiatives is a common mitigation activity. Hindering of a worsened situation is important. GEORGIA 2016-2019 and 2020-2023 The CoE's Action plans for Georgia is funded by several donors. For the action plan 2020-2023, Sweden contributed with €1.8 million. The Action plan contributed to the SDG Agenda 2030 by supporting goals 4, 5, 10, 11 and 16. HUMAN RIGHTS • Georgia having obtained candidate status for EU membership in December 2023, one of the priorities for Georgia was the effectiveness of the European Convention on Human Rights. • The legal package on legislative mechanisms ensuring reference to the European Court's decisions was adopted. This priority was assessed as completed by the European Commission. • A National Strategy for the Protection of Human Rights 2022-2030 was adopted, marking an important development. Despite its insufficient results, it aims at implementing the standards of the Istanbul Convention. • Another priority was gender equality, combating violence against women and domestic violence. This priority was considered met according to the European Commissions Annual report on Georgia, November 2023. One concrete outcome from this progress is data-based evidence that sexual violence was more reported and that cases were handled in such a way that perpetrators received punishment. RULE OF LAW • The Criminal Procedure Code was reviewed together with stakeholders, and legal aid services were implemented in smaller municipalities with higher concentration of minority populations. • The Legal Aid Council adopted quality control tools, and put in place a gender-responsive legal framework. • The judicial strategy 2017-2021, and the 4th Wave legislative package were adopted, improving the judicial appointment and accountability system in line with European standards. DEMOCRACY • Som progress was made by the introduction and consolidation of the use of civil participation methodologies as well as better ownership of human rights principles within local communities. • Another progress within democracy was the ratification of the Additional Protocol to the European Charter of Local Self-government on the right to participate in the affairs of local authority. Challenges Georgia faced increased challenges when it comes to the independence and efficiency of justice. Key recommendations have not been applied by Georgian authorities. With Parliamentary Elections coming up in 2024 , political division and polarisation could represent a risk, as criticism towards international donor organizations increases. Influential political changes made the situation for CoEs thematic areas substantially worsened after this reporting period. MOLDOVA 2017-2020 and 2021-2024 The CoE's Action plan for Moldova is funded by several donors. For action plan 2021-2024, Sweden contributed with €1.7 million. The Action plan contributed to the SDG Agenda 2030 by supporting goals 4, 5, 8, 10, 11 and 16. Some reported outcomes: HUMAN RIGHTS • Moldova was granted the status of candidate for EU membership in 2022 and access to negotiations opened the year after. • Moldova created a national programme for preventing and combating violence against women and domestic violence, and ratified the Istanbul Convention. • In order to ensure the monitoring of the refugee crisis following the full scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation, legal professionals received training in European human rights standards on migration and asylum. • Good progress was also achieved in the area of childrens rights as training allowed criminal justice professionals to increased their capacities to effectively investigate, prosecute and sentence perpetrators of crimes against children. Other groups working with children were equipped with gender-sensitive tools needed to identify and report child sexual exploitation and abuse. RULE OF LAW The amendment of the electoral legislation in line with CoEs recommendations was an achievement along with the strengthening of the legal framework for the independence of judges. DEMOCRACY The Code of Conduct for electoral actors was revised in order to combat hate speech and sexism during local elections in 2023. Good progress was achieved by the enhancement of voter awareness of the electoral process. Challenges Moldova was the biggest host of Ukrainian refugees per capita following the full scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation. This posed one of the biggest challenges for the country during the implementation of the ongoing action plan.. Adaptations to the action plan allowed for good results during the implementation of 2023. Hybrid threats was a growing concern influencing all work 2023 onwards. UKRAINE 2028-2022 and 2023-2026 The CoE's Action plan for Ukraine is funded by several donors. For action plan 2023-2026, Sweden contributed with €2.2 million. The Action plan contributed to the SDG Agenda 2030 by supporting goals 4, 5, 10, 11 and 16. The CoEs work in Ukraine was marked by the consequences of the Russian Federations full scale invasion of the country, having to shift priorities and address the need of constant coordination with other countries. With Ukraine accessing the CoEs Development Bank at no cost, loans and support worth €100 million was granted to Ukraines healthcare needs. Some reported outcomes: HUMAN RIGHTS • Ukraine was granted the status of candidate for EU membership and access negotiations opened in 2023. • Good progress was made reinforcing the rights of children, a longstanding priority in Ukraine. Actions taken, like supporting the draft law on child-friendly justice, were in line with the Lanzarote convention. • Good progress was also achieved in the area of protecting freedom of expression and media, where specific emphasis was put on the safety and protection of journalists, including in times of war. The ratification of the Convention on Access to Official Documents also enhanced the legislative framework to ensure access to public information. • Extensive support and capacity building was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor General, the Supreme Court, the judiciary in general, civil society and social service staff with the purpose of strengthening the capacity to deal with alleged crimes and human rights violations in times of war. • Yet another good progress was the ratification of the Istanbul Convention, which supported the capacity building of first-line professionals working with victims of sexual violence. • As a result of policy changes and capacity building at local level, the protection of the rights of Internally Displaced Persons (IDPs) was improved. RULE OF LAW • Some progress was achieved in the judiciary reform process, where an Ethics Council to tackle the issue of functioning of the High Council Judges and the integrity of its members was established. • The CoE provided expert support and technical assistance during the process that led to the adoption of a new law on national minorities. • A new media law was approved and after some adjustments, deemed in line with the EU aguis. DEMOCRACY • One of the priorities for Ukraines readiness for access to EU was the decentralisation reform. In line with this, the Congress of Local and Regional Authorities continuously promoted the inclusion of local authorities in the reconstruction and recovery of Ukraine. • With the aim to ensure the implication of citizens when the governance methods implied by the war (martial law) are over, the CoE supported good governance and public reforms that reflect a future transition to civilian regime. • Advocacy for the draft law no. 4254 on public consultations, and for the draft law no. 7283 on amendments to the Law of Ukraine on Local Self-Government in Ukraine, was supported in accordance with CoEs standards and recommendations. Challenges The full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation brought serious geopolitical and security risks. In this challenging context, adjustments had to be done considering new circumstances, priorities and needs at national level. Communication and coordination with other countries proved crucial. Security measures were implemented to allow in-person activities, nevertheless the war affected the engagement of national partners and stakeholders. Many organisations had to reconfigure their staff and priorities, which complicated the implementation of projects. New costs emerged that slowed down the work of CSOs. Despite all challenges, the Ukrainian authorities showed strong commitment to the implementation of the CoEs activities in the country. CONCLUSION The action plans 2019-2023 were developed and implemented in areas where the Council of Europe has strong expertise and added value to other actors. The CoE thus provides both expert support and peer-to-peer knowledge. The action plans mainstream gender equality, and contribute to the achievement of various SDG goals from Agenda 2030 in the target countries. The CoE's work has contributed to the achievement of results in some specific areas, in all countries. Some of these are: • Moving forwards with gender equality, preparing the ground for the Istanbul convention. • Advancing in the area of anti-corruption and money laundry • Strengthening Human Rights and ensuring Human Rights of refugees • Addressing Discrimination and penitentiary reforms. Sida has systematically worked to influence CoEs work with result reporting and result monitoring, with dialogue and coordination with Sweden's Embassies, and with issues related to CoEs system for audit and time reporting. Substantial process and end results have been identified on all three areas during the period. The dialogue areas will remain in focus in Sida's management of the new framework agreement made in November 2023.
No indicator available - only a description of the activity results is published
